19: Europe's 14th-century Renaissance used reason for human welfare. Bengal looked alike: priests, no modern schooling, birth privilege, poverty. So reformers took the best of scripture and used reason on the rest.

After 1813 Liberals, Utilitarians and Evangelists backed Western education and reform. Evangelist conversion scared Indians into reforming from within. Education (1835) gave the Doctrine of Reason. Bengal led because the Governor General sat there.
Religion ruled social life, so reform had to reinterpret religion. Derozio's Young Bengal used only logic and failed with the masses. Reformers used logic found inside scripture instead.

Roy, Father of Modern India, found monotheism in the Upanishads and used reason against Karma and Incarnation. He worked with Bentinck 28-35, Macaulay and David Hare. He wanted a free Press and Trial by jury.
Bentinck 28-35 demanded scriptural proof. In 1828 the Brahmo Samaj beat Radhakanta Deb in debate, and in 1829 Regulation XVII made Sati culpable homicide. Deb's Privy Council appeal failed in 1830.

Brahmo Samaj (1828) stayed upper-caste and urban. After Roy died in 1833, Debendranath Tagore held it together. Keshab Chandra Sen wanted a mass movement, so 1866 split it; the 1878 marriage of his minor daughter split it again.

Paramhansa Mandali (1849) failed like Young Bengal. The Prarthana Samaj (1867) was Brahmoism for Maharashtra. Ranade built the Poona Sarvajanik Sabha. Phule spoke for the oppressed: girls' school 1848, Satyashodhak Samaj (1873).

Child marriage had religious sanction, so the IPC 1860 set only age 10. After Phulmoni's death, Lansdowne 88-94 raised it to 12 in 1891. The Female Infanticide Act 1870 could not reach dowry or neglect of girls.

Vidyasagar opened 25 girls' schools in 1857-58, and the Widow Remarriage Act came on 26 July 1856. But widows lost property and orthodox Hindus won the debate. Early reform was elite, top-down, gradual and silent on caste.

Dayanand's Arya Samaj (1875) held the Vedas infallible. Vivekananda accepted idols and won the masses. Revivalism turned aggressive too. Sir Syed built Aligarh (1875); Narayana Guru consecrated an Ezhava's Shiva (1888).

Orientalists (Warren Hastings 73-85, Jones, Wellesley 98-05) lost to Macaulay's Minute of 1835: English, Western syllabus, Brown Sahibs. Wood's Despatch 1854 built the ladder, yet by 1921 only about 8% were Western educated.

The press began in 1780 with Hicky's Bengal Gazette; Warren Hastings 73-85 shut it in 1782. Repression and concession alternated. The educated few used the press, and Brown Sahibs became leaders of the national movement.
20: The WEMC trusted British rule and chose reform. Peasants and tribals, at the bottom of the colonial order, answered with defiance and often violence. The common man wants security.
The Farming System 1772 auctioned revenue; PS1793 made the zamindar owner with high rents and no occupancy right. Ryotwari and Mahalwari led from auction to moneylender to landlessness.
The planter's loan and cheap indigo buy-back left the ryot unable to pay rent and loan, so he grew indigo again. Bengal Ryoti brought the Indigo Revolt 1859; Bihar Tinkathia, Champaran 1917.
Temple and mosque lands were taxed, and Sati 1829, Lex Loci 1850 and Widow Remarriage 1856 felt like interference. With no parties or newspapers, a sect already had a leader, a philosophy and unity.
Tribals lived by cultivation, hunting and gathering under their own chief. British land revenue came in by four routes, with cash demands and a ban on Jhum and hunting, to make settled peasants.

Under Lytton 76-80 the Forests Act 1878 made Reserved, Protected and Village forests, mainly for railway timber. Customary rights became privileges and tribals became trespassers. The Abkari liquor monopoly added more burden.
Raja Chait Singh lost his estates (1778-81). Wazir Ali 97-98, the Poligars, the Bundelas and Veluthampi (1809) lost status, land or autonomy. The Paikas (1817) drew multi-class support.
In 1783 Rangpur peasants, hurt by the Farming System and famine, looted the grain stores of Debi Singh and Gobinda Singh and ran their own government. Mysore peasants (1830-31) rose against high LR.

Dasnami Sanyasis and Madari Fakirs inspire Anandamath. Karim and Tipu Shah lead the Pagal Panthis. Titu Mir builds a bamboo fort, the Faraizi say land belongs to God, and Moplahs lose rights to Janmies.

Pahariya, Bhil, Ramosi, Khasi, Kol and Kandh risings came from loss of land, forest or religion. The Santhals (1855-56) rose against British, zamindars and moneylenders; about 50,000 were killed, then a land-transfer bar followed.

Birsa Munda's Ulugulan (1899-1900) began on Christmas 1899, believing British bullets turn to water. Rampa merged into the NCM in 1920. Alluri Sitarama Raju restarted the Fituri and was executed in 1924.

The revolts were local, uncoordinated and had no democratic goal, so not modern nationalism. Yet they had ideology, programme and symbolism. So: the pre-history of modern nationalism, a hundred years before 1857.
